wind-chill.short: The calm-air temperature that would take heat from bare skin at the same rate as the real wind does. It describes heat loss from skin, not the real air temperature.

vasoconstriction.short: Narrowing of blood vessels. In the skin it cuts blood flow, so less heat reaches the surface and less is lost. Opposite of vasodilation.

shivering.short: Fast, involuntary muscle contractions that turn fuel into heat instead of movement. It makes a lot of heat but costs a lot of energy.

nonshivering-thermogenesis.short: Heat made without muscle movement, mainly in brown fat, where the cell's mitochondria release energy as heat instead of making ATP.

brown-adipose-tissue.short: Fat tissue packed with mitochondria that burns fuel to make heat. Adults have small amounts, and cold switches it on. Also called brown fat or BAT.

cold-habituation.short: A weaker response to the same cold after repeated exposure, for example less gasping or shivering. It turns down the alarm; it does not mean you lose less heat.

exercise-induced-bronchoconstriction.short: Narrowing of the airways during or after hard exercise, causing cough, wheeze or tight chest. Breathing cold, dry air makes it more likely. Short: EIB.

fev1.short: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second: the litres of air you can blow out in the first second after a full breath. A fall of 10% or more after hard exercise points to EIB.

hypothermia.short: Core temperature below 35 °C, because the body loses more heat than it makes. Shivering, thinking and movement get worse as it falls.

frostbite.short: Damage from freezing of the skin and the tissue under it, mostly in fingers, toes, ears and nose. The skin first feels cold, then painful, then numb.

cold-shock-response.short: A gasp, fast uncontrollable breathing, racing heart and high blood pressure in the first seconds of cold-water immersion. It peaks in about 30 s and fades by about 2 min.

swim-failure.short: The point where a swimmer in cold water can no longer swim effectively: strokes get shorter, the stroke rate rises and the body sinks lower, long before the core is very cold.

afterdrop.short: A further fall in core temperature after leaving cold water, as the cold arms, legs and outer tissues keep drawing heat from the core.

autonomic-conflict.short: A theory that the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves act on the heart at the same time (for example cold shock plus breath-holding), which can set off a dangerous heart rhythm in people with a heart condition.
